DoS Hulk.title: DoS Hulk
DoS Hulk.summary_plain: Your server was flooded with a huge volume of fake HTTP requests using a tool called HULK.
DoS Hulk.how_it_works: Your server was flooded with a huge volume of fake HTTP requests using a tool called HULK. The server may crash, restart, or become unresponsive. Databases connected to the server may also be affected.
DoS Hulk.why_it_matters: Your application becomes slow or completely unavailable during the attack. Every minute of downtime costs revenue and damages user trust. E-commerce or SaaS outages can mean direct financial loss.

Configure rate-limiting on your load balancer or API gateway.

Use a CDN to absorb and filter malicious traffic before it reaches your origin.
recovery: Validate services from known-good backups after containment.

PortScan.title: PortScan

PortScan.how_it_works: An attacker (or automated tool) systematically tried to find open doors into your server. Any unpatched service discovered during the scan becomes a potential entry point.
PortScan.why_it_matters: A port scan is reconnaissance — it means someone is actively mapping your infrastructure before attempting a deeper attack. Left unresponded, it often precedes a targeted intrusion attempt.

Repeated connections to sensitive ports from unfamiliar sources

Block the source IP at your firewall or WAF immediately.
Audit which ports are open — close anything not required for your application.

Set up rate-limiting or fail2ban to auto-block IPs that scan multiple ports.
recovery: Validate services from known-good backups after containment.

DDoS.title: DDoS

DDoS.how_it_works: Thousands of different machines (often infected computers in a botnet) are simultaneously sending traffic to overwhelm your application. Unlike a regular DoS, the attack comes from many sources at once — making it much harder to block. Your network bandwidth, server CPU, and connection tables are saturated. Even upstream providers (CDN, DNS) can be affected. All services on the same infrastructure are at risk.
DDoS.why_it_matters: Your application goes offline for real users. A sustained DDoS can last hours or days. For revenue-generating applications this is an emergency-level event. It may also be a distraction while attackers attempt a secondary breach.

Contact your ISP or cloud provider — they can filter at the network level.
containment: Enable anycast routing to distribute attack traffic across multiple data centres.
Implement IP reputation lists to block known botnet IP ranges.
recovery: Validate services from known-good backups after containment.

DoS GoldenEye.title: DoS GoldenEye

DoS GoldenEye.how_it_works: An attacker used the GoldenEye tool to send many simultaneous HTTP GET/POST requests, keeping connections open and waiting — slowly draining your server's connection capacity. It's designed to be harder to detect than volume-based attacks. Your HTTP server's connection pool is depleted. Each open connection holds server memory and a thread/process. New requests queue and eventually time out.
DoS GoldenEye.why_it_matters: Your application becomes progressively slower until it can no longer accept new connections. Legitimate users see timeouts and errors.

Limit the number of connections per IP at the load balancer level.
containment: Enable Cloudflare or similar reverse proxy to detect and block HTTP-layer DoS.
Block the source IP immediately.
recovery: Validate services from known-good backups after containment.

DoS slowloris.title: DoS slowloris
DoS slowloris.summary_plain: The Slowloris attack works by opening many connections to your server and sending HTTP headers very slowly — just fast enough to avoid timeout, but never completing the request.
DoS slowloris.how_it_works: The Slowloris attack works by opening many connections to your server and sending HTTP headers very slowly — just fast enough to avoid timeout, but never completing the request. This ties up server connections until no new users can connect. Apache and older web servers are especially vulnerable. Connection tables fill up and the server stops accepting new requests, even though CPU and memory usage remain low.
DoS slowloris.why_it_matters: Your site becomes inaccessible to real users as the attacker's zombie connections consume all available connection slots.
typical_indicators: Unusual flow duration or packet rates in network telemetry
Repeated connections to sensitive ports from unfamiliar sources
immediate_actions: Preserve logs, flow captures, and LBRO evidence before changes.
Switch to or configure nginx (it handles slow connections much better than Apache).
Set RequestReadTimeout in Apache: RequestReadTimeout header=10-20,MinRate=500.
containment: Use mod_reqtimeout or mod_limitipconn (Apache) to limit per-IP connections.
Add rate limiting at the CDN/WAF layer.
recovery: Validate services from known-good backups after containment.
Monitor for repeat patterns from the same sources.

Web Attack - XSS.title: Web Attack - XSS
Web Attack - XSS.summary_plain: An attacker tried to inject malicious JavaScript code into your web pages.
Web Attack - XSS.how_it_works: An attacker tried to inject malicious JavaScript code into your web pages. If successful, this script runs in the browsers of other users who visit the affected page — like planting a spy inside every visitor's browser session. Session hijacking, cookie theft, credential harvesting from active users. The attacker runs arbitrary code in the context of your domain — bypassing same-origin protections for everything the victim can access.
Web Attack - XSS.why_it_matters: XSS can steal user session cookies (logging attackers in as victims), redirect users to phishing sites, capture keystrokes including passwords, or deface your website. This directly damages user trust and can trigger GDPR/CCPA breach notification obligations.

Repeated connections to sensitive ports from unfamiliar sources

Implement a strict Content Security Policy (CSP) header to block inline scripts.
containment: Use framework-provided escaping (React, Angular auto-escape by default — avoid dangerouslySetInnerHTML).
Set HttpOnly and Secure flags on session cookies to prevent JavaScript theft.
recovery: Validate services from known-good backups after containment.

Web Attack - Sql Injection.title: Web Attack - Sql Injection

Heartbleed.title: Heartbleed
Heartbleed.summary_plain: The Heartbleed attack exploits a famous bug in OpenSSL (the software that powers HTTPS encryption).
Heartbleed.how_it_works: The Heartbleed attack exploits a famous bug in OpenSSL (the software that powers HTTPS encryption). By sending a crafted request, an attacker can read 64KB of memory from your server at a time — repeatedly — leaking secrets including private SSL keys and user session data. Server memory exposed. SSL private keys, session tokens, cookies, and plaintext passwords of recently logged-in users can all be read from memory. Full TLS compromise.
Heartbleed.why_it_matters: If your private SSL/TLS key is stolen, attackers can decrypt all past and future HTTPS traffic, impersonate your server, and intercept user credentials. This is a catastrophic breach requiring immediate certificate revocation.
typical_indicators: Unusual flow duration or packet rates in network telemetry
Repeated connections to sensitive ports from unfamiliar sources
immediate_actions: Preserve logs, flow captures, and LBRO evidence before changes.
Update OpenSSL to 1.0.1g or later IMMEDIATELY — this vulnerability was patched in 2014.
If you're running a vulnerable version, assume your private key is compromised.
containment: Revoke and reissue all SSL/TLS certificates.
Force all users to log out and reset session tokens.
recovery: Validate services from known-good backups after containment.
